newsitem.title: FRANCE: French economy seen plagued by high unemployment.
newsitem.headline: French economy seen plagued by high unemployment.

text.p: Near-record unemployment will plague France over the next couple of years as economic growth remains too subdued to shorten jobless queues, a Reuter poll of economists showed on Thursday.

France's inability to break out of a stubborn cycle of high unemployment which is hitting consumer confidence and growth was highlighted again on Thursday by government figures showing consumer spending fell 1.5 percent in September from August.
The Reuter poll forecast an average unemployment rate of 12.5 percent in 1996 and 1997, barely lower than the current record level of 12.6 percent.
In the second quarter of 1998, economists predicted the rate would drop marginally to 12.2 percent.

The average prediction for year-on-year gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 1997 was 2.2 percent after just 1.2 percent this year. By the second quarter of 1998, it is expected to pick up to 2.7 percent year-on-year.
Many economists reckon France would need growth of near to three percent to lower unemployment and make up for years of weak economic growth since the start of the decade.
"It's fundamentally a cyclical problem. The labour market in France is flexible enough, the problem is too poor growth rates," ABN-Amro economist Philippe Brossard said.
The forecasts offer cold comfort to France's deeply unpopular conservative government, which is straining to cut its deficit in preparation for European monetary union in 1999.

It must bring its deficit to three percent or less of GDP by 1997 to qualify for EMU and its efforts to achieve this, combined with persistent structural rigidities in the French labour market, have braked the economy, economists said.

Economists said that budgetary restraint would ease somewhat next year after the government decided to use pension fund money from state-owned France Telecom to reach the three percent target next year.
"The fiscal tightening in 1997 is far less severe than in 1996 because of the France Telecom factor," Brossard said.
The government is taking a 37.5 billion franc ($7.29 billion) transfer from the French telephone operator in exchange for the assumption of pension liabilities ahead of a planned privatisation.
But the need to keep deficits low after 1997 will keep budgets constricted in the years to come.
"What is constraining growth is the long road of tight budget policies," Francois-Xavier Chauchat, senior fixed-income strategist at Banque Nationale de Paris, said.
"Unemployment is a lagging indicator, so even if people see a rebound in the economy, unemployment will not improve. There will be a lag."

The government, which is officially forecasting growth of 2.3 percent next year after 1.3 percent this year, is counting on a recovery in the second half of 1996, continuing into next year, to carry it to monetary union.

The poll predicts the deficit will fall to 3.2 percent in 1997 from 4.3 percent this year, but economists said France's political will was such that the government would make last-minute cuts if needed to get it down to three percent.
